title: 5 explosive intent Mistakes That Are Destroying Your fast nerve firing
description: You took the intent test. Now the five mistakes that keep fast nerves slow: the ways people practise speed that actually train slowness. Here is each one, why it feels like training, and the correction that makes your reps violent again.

scenes.narration: Twenty seconds. | Maximum intent push-ups. | You know the drill. | But today, watch yourself. | Not the count. | The quality. | Do the reps stay violent | to the final second? | Or does the intent | quietly drain away | while the reps continue? | That draining is not fatigue. | It is | one of five mistakes, | and they are the reason | most speed training | secretly trains slowness. | Count your reps, | then stay for the audit. | At the | end of this video | you will know exactly | which mistake owns you, | and how to evict it | from your next session.

beats.text: WATCH THE QUALITY, NOT THE COUNT

beats.title: DRAINING IS NOT FATIGUE
lines: It is a mistake with a name.

scenes.label: STILL THE LINE - NOW VIOLENT
scenes.sub: under 9 with mistakes running: your ceiling was method, not muscle
scenes.narration: The line from the intent test stands: fifteen full-intent reps in twenty seconds is a firing system that works. But reinterpret the low score one more time. Under nine with mistakes running does not mean slow nerves. It means nerves being trained, diligently, in the wrong direction, because the nervous system does not learn what you call the session. It learns what the session actually was. If your speed work was long, tired and ninety percent, you have been running a very consistent slowness programme with excellent attendance. The good news writes itself: stop teaching the wrong lesson and the right one lands fast.

beats.text: IT LEARNS WHAT THE SESSION WAS

scenes.narration: Mistake one: holding back to survive the set. You pace the first reps at ninety percent so the last reps exist, which feels like strategy and is actually sabotage: the nervous system records the strongest command sent, and ninety becomes the ceiling it defends. The fix is structural: sets so short that survival is never in question, twenty seconds or less, so every rep can be a genuine maximum. Mistake two: the marathon speed set. Two minutes of 'fast' reps is an oxymoron with a stopwatch; after thirty seconds the reps are slow, the intent is gone, and the session's majority is slow practice. The fix is the same shape: many short sets, full recovery, and the set ends the moment the reps lose their violence, not when the clock grants permission.

beats.title: SHORT SETS OR IT ISN'T SPEED

scenes.narration: Mistake three: skipping the rest. Speed work with short rests is conditioning wearing a costume; the firing rate you are training is a fresh nervous system's firing rate, and a tired system fires at tired speeds, which you then practise. Full recovery between sets is not laziness, it is the training. Mistake four: intent only on the easy reps. People attack the first two reps and cruise the rest, or save intent for light days. The nervous system averages the session, and the average is the adaptation. The fix is a standard, not a mood: every rep of speed work is a maximum attempt, and when maximum is unavailable, the session is over. Four mistakes down, and you may notice they are all the same mistake wearing costumes: protecting the reps instead of the quality.

One more place the mistakes hide: the warm-up. Watch how most people prepare for speed work, a few casual reps at half intent to 'save themselves' for the sets, and you are watching the nervous system being primed for the wrong gear. The warm-up is not separate from the training; it is the first training the nerves receive that day, and it votes. Prime with intent: two or three single reps at genuine maximum, fully rested, before the first set, and the system arrives at the work already speaking the right language. Prime casually and the first two sets are spent translating. At your level of practice the warm-up is short, but it is never casual. Nothing about speed is.

Mistake five: testing tired. You take the intent test at the end of a workout, or at the end of a long day, record a depressing number, and conclude your nerves are slow. You measured fatigue and filed it as ability. The nervous system's firing rate is one of the most state-dependent numbers in this entire season: sleep, stress and accumulated work all move it by whole reps. The fix is a testing ritual: same time of day, rested, after a warm-up, never after training. Respect the ritual and the number becomes a signal. Ignore it and you are charting your tiredness with great precision and learning nothing about your speed.

Now the hopeful arithmetic. | Every mistake on this list | is a behaviour, | not a body. | Behaviours change in a day. | Your first clean session | can happen tomorrow: | six short sets, | full recoveries, | every rep a maximum, | done while fresh. | And your frame rewards it | more than anyone's: | low mass means | each violent rep | stays violent longer | into the set, | so your quality seconds | outnumber the heavy lifter's | in every session. | He practises fatigue. | You can practise speed. | That difference, compounded, | is an explosive athlete.

beats.text: HE PRACTISES FATIGUE. YOU PRACTISE SPEED.

scenes.narration: Train with me. Twenty seconds of genuine maximums, forty seconds of full rest, four rounds. If a rep stops being violent, the round is over early and that is success, not failure. Go.

Your repair week: two intent sessions, fresh, never after other training, six short sets each with full recoveries and a hard quality rule. Before each session, write your worst mistake on the whiteboard of your mind and coach against it specifically: the pacer shortens his sets, the marathoner sets a timer, the rest-skipper watches the clock like it is the exercise. Retest only under ritual conditions at week's end. If maximum intent work produces sharp joint pain, or wrist and shoulder complaints that accumulate across the week, reduce the volume, and see a professional if it persists. Violent effort, clean joints: both halves are the standard. Keep a session log with one column only: quality, marked honestly out of ten. When quality and count are both recorded, the truth about a training block stops being an argument.

Retest under ritual: rested, same hour, warmed up, six honest sets behind you this week. If the count climbs, file it correctly: your nerves were never slow, your practice was. If the count holds but the last reps now stay violent to the final second, that is the deeper victory, because rep quality at the end is firing speed that survives, and the count follows it within weeks. Put your old count, your new count, and your worst mistake in the comments. Thirty-day formal retest under the same ritual closes the case, and by then the twenty seconds will feel less like a test and more like a demonstration. Grade the retest set on the final five seconds specifically. Anyone can be violent fresh. The athlete is the one whose last rep would still win an argument with the floor.

Thirty days of clean, violent, rested reps and the fast gear becomes your default gear. Short sets, full rest, every rep a maximum. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
